meta.title: Indus Script Decipherment Workbench & Sign Concordance
meta.subtitle: Interactive catalog of Harappan signs, positional frequencies, reading direction, and major decipherment hypotheses

corpus_stats.boustrophedon_rate: 7.2% (alternating R-to-L and L-to-R in multi-line texts)

theories.name: Dravidian Rebus Hypothesis
theories.proponents: Asko Parpola (Univ. of Helsinki); Iravatham Mahadevan (ASI / Epigraphical Society); Walter Fairservis
theories.framework: Logo-syllabic script where pictograms represent homonyms (rebus principle) based on Proto-Dravidian roots. For example, the fish sign (mīn) represents both 'fish' and 'star' (mīn), allowing astral deities and planetary alignments to be recorded.
theories.strengths: Supported by Brahui (a North Dravidian language surviving in Balochistan heartland), structural positional constraints, and Dravidian loanwords in the Rigveda.
theories.status: Most widely studied linguistic decipherment framework in international academia.

theories.name: Proto-Indo-Aryan / Sanskrit Hypothesis
theories.proponents: S.R. Rao (Excavator of Lothal); Natwar Jha; N.S. Rajaram
theories.framework: Argues that Mature Harappan script evolved into an alphabetic or consonantal writing system related to early Brahmi, encoding Vedic and Proto-Sanskrit words (e.g. 'maha', 'shasa', 'arka', 'pa').
theories.strengths: Direct cultural and architectural continuities observed in fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal, swastika and yoga postures.
theories.status: Debated; criticized by many computational linguists for flexible phonetic assignments without rigid cross-checks.

theories.name: Non-Linguistic Symbolic System
theories.proponents: Steve Farmer; Richard Sproat; Michael Witzel (Harvard University, 2004)
theories.framework: Proposes that the Indus signs were non-linguistic political, religious, or clan emblems (similar to coats of arms or heraldic insignia) rather than a phonetic spoken script, pointing to the extreme brevity of inscriptions (avg. 4.6 signs).
theories.strengths: Explains why no long literary texts, clay tablets, or monumental stone histories exist despite an empire spanning 1.5 million sq. km.
theories.status: Controversial; strongly challenged by Rao et al. (Science 2009) whose conditional entropy and Markov model tests proved Indus text entropy matches spoken natural languages (Sumerian, Sanskrit, English) and differs from non-linguistic symbols.

signs.name: The Jar / Vessel Sign
signs.description: The single most frequent sign in the entire Indus corpus. Appears predominantly at the end (terminal) of inscriptions.
signs.dravidian_meaning: Vessel / Lord / Ruler / Clan suffix (nominal genitive/dative ending)

signs.name: Standard Fish Sign
signs.description: Classic fish outline. Central to the Dravidian rebus decipherment (mīn = fish and star).
signs.dravidian_meaning: Fish → homophone for 'Star / Planet / Luminary deity'

signs.name: Fish with Roof / Canopy
signs.description: Fish sign surmounted by a triangular canopy or roof diacritic.
signs.dravidian_meaning: Covered star / Saturn (Dravidian: mai-mīn = dark/slow star)

signs.name: Pectinated Fish (Finned / Star Cluster)
signs.description: Fish sign with internal transverse hatching lines resembling fins or scales.

signs.name: Four-Spoked Wheel / Sun
signs.description: Circle containing an inscribed Greek-cross (+), representing a spoked wheel or solar disc.
signs.dravidian_meaning: Disc / Wheel / Sun / Time cycle (āzi = discus/ocean)

signs.name: Man with Bow & Arrow
signs.description: Anthropomorphic stick figure holding an arched hunting bow.

signs.name: Two Vertical Strokes (Numeral 2)
signs.description: Two distinct parallel vertical strokes used as multiplier or syllable indicator.

signs.name: Three Vertical Strokes (Numeral 3)
signs.description: Three parallel vertical strokes, often indicating plural or triad.
signs.dravidian_meaning: Three / Triad (mu-mīn = three stars of Orion)

signs.name: Forked Horns / Tree Sign
signs.description: Upward branching forks resembling tree branches or sacred bovid horns.

signs.name: Diamond / Sieve Sign
signs.description: Lozenge or rhombus, occasionally bisected by cross-strokes.

signs.name: Lance / Spearhead Sign
signs.description: Triangular blade atop a central vertical shaft.

signs.name: Harrow / Comb Sign
signs.description: Horizontal spine with four downward pointing vertical teeth.

famous_inscriptions.title: The Dholavira 10-Character Signboard
famous_inscriptions.context: Found fallen in the western chamber of the monumental North Gateway of the Citadel. Each symbol is approximately 37 cm high, crafted from pure white crystalline gypsum inlaid into a massive wooden signboard that hung above the city gate.
famous_inscriptions.interpretation: A civic, royal, or territorial proclamation declaring the sovereign authority and divine protection of the city of Dholavira and its merchant citadel.

famous_inscriptions.title: Pashupati Seal (M-304)
famous_inscriptions.context: Discovered in Block 1, Southern Area of the Citadel by Ernest Mackay. Steatite seal depicting a three-faced horned deity seated in yogic asana (Mulabandhasana) flanked by an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, water buffalo, and antelopes.
famous_inscriptions.interpretation: Lord of the Beasts / Proto-Shiva: Dedication inscription to the master of wild creatures, divine yogic protector, and guardian of cosmic forces.

famous_inscriptions.title: Mohenjo-daro Royal Unicorn Seal (M-1)
famous_inscriptions.context: Square steatite stamp seal depicting the magnificent unicorn (Ekashringa) with arched single horn facing a sacred double-decked incense burner / filter stand. Over 65% of all IVC seals bear this exact creature.
famous_inscriptions.interpretation: Standard commercial credential of a high-ranking civic official or merchant guild overseeing exports from the Mohenjo-daro central district.

famous_inscriptions.title: Harappan Unicorn Seal at Ur (Mesopotamia)
famous_inscriptions.context: Discovered in an Akkadian royal tomb in southern Iraq by Sir Leonard Woolley. Square steatite seal cut by an authentic Harappan master carver, carried by an Indus merchant residing in Mesopotamia.
famous_inscriptions.interpretation: Proof of overseas Meluhhan merchant diaspora: credential of a Harappan trade factor living in the Meluhha quarter of southern Mesopotamia.

famous_inscriptions.title: Lothal Persian Gulf Seal & Sealing
famous_inscriptions.context: Found in the warehouse area adjacent to the Lothal tidal dock basin. Clay sealing used to stamp bundles of cotton textiles and bales of timber destined for overseas shipping.
famous_inscriptions.interpretation: Maritime customs and cargo verification stamp certifying the weight, origin, and tax payment of Indian goods leaving the Gulf of Khambhat.
